analysis.one_liner: Removes caps on individual and party campaign donations while shielding unpaid online activism from campaign-finance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have scrapped the annual cap on individual campaign contributions and freed online activism from campaign-finance rules, was referred to committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal campaign-finance law in two main ways. First, it would have repealed the annual cap on how much money one individual can give in total across all federal candidates and committees, and would have removed the dollar limits on how much national and state political parties can spend to elect candidates. Second, it would have made clear that unpaid online political activity — blogging, emailing, linking to websites — does not count as a campaign contribution, and would have extended the same legal protection newspapers get to blogs and other online publications. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee at the end of the 111th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individuals who want to give more than the aggregate limit to federal candidates and committees, and national and state political parties, which could then spend unlimited amounts in coordination with candidates. The internet provisions also benefit bloggers and online activists of all income levels, who gain legal certainty that unpaid online political activity cannot be regulated as a campaign contribution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy donors, political parties, and bloggers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the annual aggregate cap on what one individual can give across all federal candidates and non-party political committees, letting large donors give far more than the roughly $45,600 per year then permitted.
Removes statutory dollar limits on coordinated and independent election spending by national and state political parties.

Exempts unpaid online activity — blogging, forwarding emails, linking, running websites — from counting as campaign contributions or expenditures, and extends the press exemption to blogs and other online publications.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters, in the form of elections even more dependent on the largest individual donors; candidates would be incentivized to court a small pool of maximum givers. Unregulated online political spending by anyone, including large actors claiming the internet exemption, would also be harder to track.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the annual aggregate cap would allow a single wealthy donor to give the legal maximum to every federal candidate, party committee, and political committee each year, magnifying the political voice of the largest donors relative to everyone else.

Removing statutory limits on party coordinated and independent expenditures would allow national and state parties to spend unlimited sums in coordination with candidates, channeling more big money through party structures.

The bill's broad internet exemption applies not only to individuals but also to wholly-owned corporations, which critics could argue stretches the 'uncompensated online activity' carve-out beyond its stated blogger-protection purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The blogger and online-activist protections were a real, low-cost fix to an ambiguity that could have subjected unpaid internet commentary to campaign-finance rules. But that provision was packaged with the bill's core change: eliminating the aggregate cap on individual contributions and lifting party spending limits, which would concentrate even more influence over campaigns with the biggest donors. The modest free-speech benefit does not offset the cost of removing the main federal check on very large individual donations; a narrower bill limited to the internet exemption would have weighed much better.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Committee on House Administration, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2010, roughly five weeks before the midterm elections, and referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or consideration in the Senate.
It attracted no cosponsors, indicating it did not build support even within the sponsor's own party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed the law, so the existing limits on individual contributions and party spending stayed in place; donors seeking to give more and parties seeking to spend more lost nothing but gained nothing either, and the ambiguity around unpaid online activism also went unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing donor and party spending limits

for.name: Rep. Tom Cole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 29, 2010, less than six weeks before the midterm elections.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or report was held, so it never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a single Republican with no cosponsors of either party and never advanced far enough for a partisan split to show up in any vote.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy households
industries.note: The bill lifts the annual aggregate ceiling on individual contributions, letting the biggest donors spread maximum checks across every candidate and committee. Ordinary donors who give small amounts see no change.
Parties would gain unlimited authority to spend money in coordination with candidates, increasing the leverage of national and state party organizations over elections.

industries.industry: Online publishers, bloggers, and internet activists
industries.note: Unpaid internet political activity would be clearly shielded from being counted as campaign contributions or expenditures, and blogs would receive the same media exemption as newspapers. This small, genuine free-speech benefit runs alongside the public's interest.
By removing contribution and party-spending limits, the bill narrows the terrain the Federal Election Commission can regulate, weakening one of the main legal checks on campaign money.
